ns2:section.sectionText: Semantics is the study of meaning and knowledge of semantics is important for the understanding of everyday language. Computational Semantics provides models for the creation of various kinds of advanced tools of natural language processing, with application to machine translation, automatic indexing, (multilingual) question answering, text coherence, image understanding, and so on. This course provides an introduction to some of the major concepts and recent developments in the computational semantics of natural language from both a theoretical linguistics and a language engineering perspective. It introduces material that is relevant to linguistics, computer science and engineering. Topics include various representation schemes required for semantic analysis beyond word meaning, with focus on polysemy, metonymy, predicate-argument structure, intentionality, discourse, and world knowledge. Students will become familiar with the techniques and tools needed to develop semantic-based systems such as semantic parsing, with application to question answering, textual entailment, and text-to-scene/Image generation. If time permits, the course will also cover advanced issues, such as techniques and challenges in the semantic processing of multilingual corpora. Organization: Lecture presentations and guided discussions will take place based on reading of prepared material. Case studies and examples will be used to illustrate the practical application of the main concepts, methods, and tools. Students will work on a project of their choice or on a default project introduced at the beginning of the semester. Prerequisites: The course is open to all students interested in advanced topics in computational linguistics. Background in at least one of the following (or equivalent) courses is required: LING 406 (Introduction to Computational Linguistics), CS 498 (Introduction to Natural Language Processing), CS 546 (Machine Learning and Natural Language), ECE 594 (Mathematical Models of Language), CS 225 (Data Structures), or CS 273 (Theory of Computation). Undergraduate students can take the course with the consent of the instructor.
